title: Quantum Enhanced Deep Reinforcement Learning for Distribution Network Reconfiguration
authors: Daniel Germain, Mason Blanchard, Audrey Versteegen, Nora Bauer, Jonathan Mei, Claudio Girotto, Paul Smith, Martin Roetteler
abstract: Modern smart grids generate increasingly rich operational data and deploy greater numbers of remotely controlled switching assets than ever before, creating new opportunities for data-driven distribution network reconfiguration (DNR). DNR optimizes grid topology to improve efficiency, reduce power losses, and maintain operational constraints, but finding optimal switch configurations remains a computationally demanding combinatorial problem. In this paper, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for static DNR to systematically investigate how the Q-network architecture affects both solution quality and learning performance. We evaluate multiple architectures within a controlled DRL framework, varying only the Q-network to isolate the contribution of each architectural choice. Our results show that quantum-enhanced Q-networks can achieve higher rewards with fewer parameters than their classical counterpart, suggesting that such architectures are a promising direction for combinatorial power systems optimization.
summary: This paper tackles the computationally hard problem of optimizing smart grid distribution networks using Deep Reinforcement Learning. They propose a novel quantum-enhanced DRL approach, replacing classical network layers with quantum circuits. The results show that this hybrid quantum-classical model can solve the optimization problem effectively while requiring fewer parameters than purely classical deep learning models.
main_problem: Optimizing the complex, NP-hard combinatorial problem of Distribution Network Reconfiguration (DNR) in smart grids.
main_result: Quantum-enhanced Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) networks can achieve competitive performance with significantly fewer trainable parameters compared to classical counterparts.
method: A hybrid Double DQN framework is employed, replacing the classical MLP backbone of the Q-network with a Parameterized Quantum Circuit (PQC).
model_or_system: The system modeled is an electrical distribution network (IEEE 33 and 69 bus systems) whose optimal topology must be found by sequentially modifying switch states.
key_observables: Mean final reward, line loss (MW), voltage profiles, and the number of trainable parameters.
important_parameters: Learning rate, discount factor, exploration parameters, and the number of qubits/circuit width (e.g., 12-qubit model).
main_assumptions: The performance comparison is made between simulated and hardware-executed results on a trapped-ion quantum processor (IonQ Forte Enterprise-1).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the DRL training procedure (replay buffer, Bellman target) and compare initial vs. post-reconfiguration voltage profiles on both ideal simulation and IonQ hardware.
paper_structure: The paper establishes DNR as an RL problem, details the DQL/DDQN framework, proposes the quantum enhancement, and evaluates performance metrics (reward, parameters) across different network sizes and hardware platforms.
why_interesting: The work directly applies quantum computation (PQC) to solve a complex, real-world optimization problem, demonstrating a potential quantum advantage in parameter efficiency for hybrid ML models.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The deep reinforcement learning training procedure used in this work. Transitions are generated through interaction with a simulated distribution network and are stored in the replay buffer. The replay buffer is sampled to train the online Q-network. The online and target networks are used to construct the Bellman target, which is compared with the predicted action value to compute the training loss.
Fig. 2. IEEE 33-bus distribution system in its initial radial configuration. Each line is modeled as switchable, with five switches initially open and the remaining switches closed.

Fig. 3. Double decision-head architecture used to implement the branch-exchange operation. The shared backbone representation is first passed to the closing head to score candidate closing actions. The closing-head output is then combined with the shared representation and passed to the opening head, allowing the opening decision to depend on the preceding closing decision.

Fig. 4. Parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) architecture used for each quantum layer of the quantum MLP. Each PQC consists of a data-embedding stage followed by a variational ansatz with four layers in all experiments. The complete quantum backbone consists of four sequential PQC layers of this form.

Fig. 5. Power-flow reward (voltage and loss terms, no exploration bonus) against line loss for 22 radial IEEE 33-bus configurations. Reward parameters for this curve are listed in Table II of the Appendix.
